summary: A fairly quiet day: Ford says Canada should plan for lasting U.S. tariffs, Poilievre pitches tariff-free autos in Detroit, and September inflation (Oct. 19) is next for the Bank of Canada.
body: Canada–U.S. trade is still stuck. Formal talks have been paused since August, when Prime Minister Mark Carney called them off over what he called unreasonable U.S. demands. The U.S. charges 25% on Canadian cars, and Trump has threatened to double that on Jan. 1[^2]. On Wednesday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford told a Toronto audience that Canada should "plan as if tariffs are here for good," even after Trump leaves office[^1]. A day earlier, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit meeting auto industry and union people to push for tariff-free car trade. He rejected the idea that the visit, a few weeks before the Nov. 3 U.S. midterms, interferes in U.S. politics[^2].

On the economy, the next big number is September inflation, due Monday, Oct. 19[^7]. In August, prices were up 3.0% from a year earlier. Gasoline was up about 23% and pushed the number up, while the core measures the Bank of Canada watches were near its 2% target[^5]. Jobs are weaker: Canada lost about 68,000 jobs in September, and unemployment rose to 6.5%[^4]. Young people aged 15 to 24 lost 48,000 jobs, and their unemployment rate stayed around 13%[^3]. The Bank's key rate is 2.25%, and its next decision is Oct. 28[^6][^11]. A small-business group (CFIB) expects growth to slow to 1.4% in the fourth quarter, and many of its members plan to raise prices[^8].

In Toronto, workers began removing the Bloor Street West bike lanes in Etobicoke under a provincial plan, and two protesters were arrested. Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says "these bike lanes are coming out"[^9]. Toronto's municipal election is Monday, Oct. 26. More than 220,000 people voted in advance polls, the highest advance turnout since 1998[^10].
differences: Bike lanes: the Ontario government calls removing them traffic relief. Critics, including Mayor Olivia Chow, call it provincial overreach and a waste of money. An engineering report the province itself paid for found that congestion benefits would be small or short-lived, and that the lanes cut crashes by 35–50%. The city estimates removal at $48 million; the province disputes that figure but has not published its own. Mayoral challenger Brad Bradford supports removing the Etobicoke lanes[^9].
